section.p: Section gave the derivative at one point. For example,
That number is the slope of one tangent line. But a curve has many points, and the slope usually changes from point to point. If the point moves, the derivative moves with it.
So the derivative is not only a number. It is also a new function.

exercise.title: Why may the domain of f' be smaller than the domain of f?

statement.p: The function f(x)=|x| is defined for every real x, but f'(0) does not exist. In your own words, why can a derivative function omit points that the original function includes?

hint.p: f' is defined only where the limiting slope exists. Existence of a height is a weaker demand than existence of a single nearby slope.

warning.title: A caution about \dfrac{dy}{dx}
warning.p: At this stage, it means a limit of such quotients. It is not introduced as an ordinary fraction of two real numbers.
In the next section, dx and dy will acquire a useful meaning through linear approximation.

exercise.title: Why is the derivative a function and not only a number?

statement.p: At one point, f'(a) is a tangent slope. If the point is allowed to move, we write f'(x). In your own words, what new object is this, and how does its graph differ in meaning from the graph of f?

hint.p: The original graph records height. The derivative graph records slope at each x where the limit exists.

subsection.title: Reading f' from the graph of f
subsection.p: The graph of f contains the graph of f' in hidden form. At each x, the value f'(x) is the slope of the tangent line to the graph of f.
This gives several visual rules.

md.mrow: \begin{array}{c|c} feature of f \amp meaning for f'
f\text{ has a horizontal tangent} \amp f'(x)=0
f\text{ has a sharp corner} \amp f'(x)\text{ may not exist} \end{array}

exercise.title: How does the graph of f hide the graph of f'?

statement.p: Rising, falling, a horizontal tangent, and a sharp corner each have a meaning for f'. In your own words, how would you read those features from the graph of f, and why does the graph of f' not show the height of f?

hint.p: At each x, the value of f' is a slope, not a height. Sign, size, and existence of that slope are what the original graph can reveal.

subsection.title: Reading f from the graph of f'
subsection.p: The derivative graph also gives information in the opposite direction.
If f'(x)>0, then the tangent slopes are positive, so f is rising.
If f'(x)<0, then the tangent slopes are negative, so f is falling.
If f'(x)=0, then the graph of f has a horizontal tangent.

This is why derivatives help us understand graphs. A derivative is local information, but when we collect it point by point, it begins to describe the whole curve.

paragraphs.title: What f' does not tell by itself
paragraphs.p: The derivative does not remember vertical shifts.
The two graphs have the same slopes at corresponding x-values, but one graph is 5 units higher.

note.title: The derivative forgets constants
note.p: A derivative records change. Adding a constant changes height, but not slope.

paragraphs.p: This points toward the second half of calculus. If we know all the slopes f'(x), how much of f can we recover? We will eventually need a starting value and a way to accumulate slope information.
Before that larger question, we use the derivative for a more local purpose: near one point, a curve can be replaced by a line.

exercise.title: Why does the derivative forget vertical shifts?

statement.p: The functions x^2 and x^2+5 have the same derivative. In your own words, why must that happen, and what information about f is therefore missing from f' alone?

hint.p: Adding a constant changes height, not slope. Recovering a function from its slopes will later need a starting value.
